Percentages are calculated based on the total number of included studies (n=707) unless otherwise specified. Categories are not mutually exclusive. Functional outcomes were defined as measures of visual function, primarily best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA). Anatomical outcomes were defined as structural measures of retinal morphology assessed by optical coherence tomography (OCT), including central retinal thickness (CRT), central macular thickness (CMT), intraretinal fluid (IRF), and subretinal fluid (SRF). thereby providing researchers with a structured reference to better inform future trial design. Prior research in this domain has predominantly centered on screening strategies and outcome pre-diction (25, 26). To date, however, no systematic review has specifically examined the methodological and design characteristics of interventional clinical trials for diabetic retinopathy. To our knowledge, the present study therefore constitutes the first com-prehensive assessment of diabetic retinopathy clinical trial features. Clinical research on diabetic retinopathy began to show an upward trend around 2005, coinciding with the emergence of the anti-VEGF therapeutic era. Following FDA approval of bevacizumab for oncological indications in 2004 and ranibizumab for neovascular age-related macular degeneration in 2006, the ophthalmology community rapidly initiated exploratory intravitreal injection studies. This paradigm shift fundamentally transformed DR/DME treatment, where laser photocoagulation had previously been the sole standard of care (27).This therapeutic shift stimulated substan-tial clinical investigations into the efficacy, safety, and dosing regimens of anti-VEGF agents. Concurrently, the progressive adop-tion of optical coherence tomography (OCT) provided a standard-ized tool for objective quantitative assessment of retinal thickness, lowering the imaging threshold for clinical trials and further contributing to research growth (28). Between 2005 and 2017, DR clinical research maintained steady growth driven by landmark multicenter trials from the DRCR.net (e.g., Protocol I in 2012 establishing ranibizumab plus laser as standard DME therapy, and Protocol T in 2015 comparing ranibizumab, aflibercept, and bevacizumab) (29, 30). chunks.document_content: Real-world injection burden, treatment switching, and visual outcomes in diabetic macular edema: a 563-eye cohort study Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS soft­ ware (version 25.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were presented as mean ± stan­ dard deviation, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Normality of distribution was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Within-group comparisons of baseline and 12-month BCVA were performed using paired t-tests. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test. The association between injection number and visual acuity change was evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Treatment switching Treatment switching from bevacizumab to aflibercept was considered in eyes demonstrating inadequate ana­ tomical or functional response. Inadequate response was defined as persistent retinal fluid, insufficient ana­ tomical improvement on OCT assessment, or lack of satisfactory functional improvement, as judged by the treating physician, despite repeated injections. Because of the retrospective real-world design, no rigid quanti­ tative anatomical or visual acuity thresholds were pre­ defined; treatment switching decisions were based on the treating physician's overall clinical judgment integrat­ ing both anatomical and functional response. For eyes undergoing treatment switching, the timing of switching, BCVA before switching, and BCVA after switching were recorded. Treatment switching was unidirectional from bevacizumab to aflibercept during the 12-month study period; no eyes switched back to bevacizumab or under­ went additional therapeutic modifications. Multivariable linear regression To identify independent predictors of visual outcomes, a multivariable linear regression analysis was per­ formed. The dependent variable was change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR). Independent variables included baseline BCVA, total number of injections during the first year, and treatment switching status. Variables were selected based on clinical relevance and prior literature. Regres­ sion coefficients (β) and corresponding P values were reported. Generalized estimating equation analysis To account for potential inter-eye correlation arising from inclusion of both eyes from some patients, a gener­ alized estimating equation (GEE) model was performed using an exchangeable working correlation structure with robust standard errors. Patient identifier was specified as the clustering variable. The dependent variable was change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR), and independent variables included baseline BCVA, number of injections, treat­ ment switching status, age, and sex. Data collection Demographic and clinical data were extracted from medical records. Variables included age, sex, number of outpatient visits, total number of intravitreal injections, baseline and 12-month BCVA, and treatment switching status. BCVA was measured using Snellen charts and converted to logarithm of the minimum angle of reso­ lution (logMAR) units using standardized conversion methods. Visual acuity change (ΔlogMAR) was calcu­ lated as the difference between 12-month and baseline values, with negative values indicating visual improve­ ment. Visual outcomes were additionally categorized as improvement (decrease in BCVA of ≥ 0.1 logMAR), sta­ bility (change in BCVA between - 0.1 and + 0.1 logMAR), or deterioration (increase in BCVA of ≥ 0.1 logMAR). Sensitivity analysis As a sensitivity analysis, the regression model was repeated after restricting the dataset to one randomly selected eye per patient to assess the robustness of the findings. For subgroup analysis, eyes were stratified according to the median baseline BCVA value (1.0 log­ MAR).

In landmark randomized controlled trials such as RISE/RIDE and Protocol T, greater visual gains were achieved with more intensive and protocol-driven treatment regimens. In comparison, the magnitude of visual improvement observed in our cohort was more modest, which may reflect lower injection frequency, variability in follow-up adherence, and differences in retreatment strategies in Mean best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) improved from 0.75 ± 0.43 logMAR at baseline to 0.59 ± 0.42 log­ MAR at the 12-month assessment, representing a mean change of - 0.16 ± 0.35 logMAR (P < 0.001). Visual improvement was observed in 339 eyes (60.2%), stability in 122 eyes (21.7%), and deterioration in 102 eyes (18.1%) (Table 2). An association was observed between the total number of intravitreal injections and change in BCVA in univari­ ate analysis (Fig. 1). Treatment switching from bevacizumab to aflibercept occurred in 167 of 563 eyes (29.7%). The mean time to switching was 4.5 ± 0.7 months after treatment initiation. The distribution of switching timing is shown in Fig. 2, and additional characteristics, including subgroup analy­ ses, are summarized in Table 3.

Value Baseline BCVA (logMAR), mean ± SD 0.75 ± 0.43 12-month BCVA (logMAR), mean ± SD 0.59 ± 0.42 Change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR), mean ± SD -0.16 ± 0.35 P-value • 0.001 Improvement, n (%) 339 (60.2%) Stability, n (%) Sensitivity analysis restricted to one eye per patient showed similar results (Table 4). 122 (21.7%) Deterioration, n (%) 102 (18.1%) BCVA: best-corrected visual acuity; SD: standard deviation; ΔlogMAR: change in logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution Discussion In this large real-world cohort of patients with diabetic macular edema (DME), intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy was associated with improvement in visual acuity despite a moderate injection frequency. These findings appear to be consistent with the established role of VEGF in the pathophysiology of diabetic retinopathy and macular edema and support the effectiveness of anti-VEGF ther­ apy in routine clinical practice [3, 4]. Visual outcomes were categorized as improvement (ΔlogMAR ≤ - 0.1), stability (- 0.1 < ΔlogMAR < + 0.1), or deterioration (ΔlogMAR ≥ + 0.1) P-value represents the comparison between baseline and 12-month BCVA values Results A total of 563 eyes with diabetic macular edema were included in the analysis. The mean age of the patients was 61.2 ± 9.3 years, and 60.1% were female. All eyes completed at least 12 months of follow-up. Baseline demographic characteristics and treatment burden are summarized in Table 1. During the first year of follow-up, eyes received a mean of 5.4 ± 2.4 intravitreal injections and attended 8.0 ± 2.2 outpatient visits (Table 1). The magnitude of visual improvement observed in this study can be contextualized in relation to pivotal ran­ domized controlled trials. The RISE and RIDE studies demonstrated substantial visual gains with ranibizumab [5], while the VIVID and VISTA trials confirmed simi­ lar efficacy with aflibercept [6]. In addition, the DRCR. net Protocol T study highlighted the importance of base­ line visual acuity in determining treatment response [7]. In contrast to these trials, which employed fixed and intensive dosing regimens, patients in the present study received a mean of 5.4 injections during the first year. This lower injection frequency reflects real-world practice patterns and is consistent with previous obser­ vational studies reporting reduced treatment intensity compared with clinical trials [8, 12, 13].

chunks.document_content: Model Construction for Diabetic Mice Male wild-type C57BLKS/J mice (wild-type, 20-30 g, 8 weeks old) and C57BLKS/J db/db diabetic mice (40-60 g, 8 weeks old) were purchased from GemPharmatech LLC. (Jiangsu, China). Carrying a mutation in the leptin receptor (Lepr) gene, db/db mice spontaneously develop obesity and persistent hyperglycemia, making them a classic preclinical model for investigating DR. All animals were enrolled in experiments at 8 weeks of age, with fasting blood glucose and body weight monitored routinely. Successful establishment of diabetic phenotypes was confirmed when fasting blood glucose levels remained 13.9 mmol/L for two consecutive days (Zheng et al., 2024). To ensure full development of retinal patho­ logical lesions induced by sustained hyperglycemia, all mice were longitudinally monitored from 8 weeks to 25 weeks of age over a total follow-up period of 17 weeks. Ocular globes and intact retinal tissues were harvested after euthanasia at the 25-week experimental endpoint. Therefore, 25 weeks of age was defined as the study's terminal time point, and all retinal morphological alterations observed at this stage pre­ dominantly recapitulate DR-like injuries driven by long-standing diabetic conditions. MGC, NAMPTþMGC, and SLC40A1 þ MGC subsets according to the differential expression of signature genes unique to each cluster. Stacked grouped bar charts were generated to quantify and visualize the proportional composition of each microglial subpopu­ lation in DR and normal samples. Differential Expression and Functional Enrichment Analyses The FindMarkers function within the Seurat toolkit was utilized to screen differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across discrete microglial subpopulations, with statistical significance assessed via the Wilcoxon rank-sum test; genes passing adjusted p-value thresh­ olds were defined as statistically significant DEGs. Genes with prominent upregulation specifically enriched in SLC40A1 þ MGC were extracted as core candidates for subsequent functional exploration. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses were completed using the R package clusterProfiler. Enrichment outputs covered three hierarchical GO categories (biological process, molecular function, cellular component) alongside KEGG pathways, and top enriched functional terms were visualized in bubble plots. Microglia-specific SLC40A1 conditional knockout mice were generated via the tamoxifen-inducible Cx3cr1-CreERT2 Cre-loxP recombination system and provided by Shanghai Model Organisms Center, Inc. (China). Briefly, loxP sites were inserted flanking the functionally critical exons of the SLC40A1 locus to generate SLC40A1flox/flox mice, which were subse­ quently crossed with Cx3cr1-CreERT2 mice. Under transcriptional control of the Cx3cr1 promoter, CreERT2 recombinase was selectively expressed within microglial and myeloid cell lineages. After induction, CreERT2 mediated deletion of the targeted SLC40A1 fragment flanked by loxP sites, yielding Cx3cr1-CreERT2; SLC40A1flox/flox conditional knockout mice. To dissect the biological role of microglial SLC40A1 during DR progression, two experimental cohorts were established on the db/db diabetic background, with eight mice allocated to each group (n 1⁄4 8). The db/db-NC group consisted of littermate control mice carrying the corresponding control genotype, while the db/db-SLC40A1-/- group contained microglia-specific conditional SLC40A1 knockout mice gener­ ated via Cx3cr1-CreERT2-mediated recombination on Pseudotime Trajectory Analysis Pseudotime trajectory reconstruction with Monocle2 was performed to delineate dynamic state transitions among distinct microglial subpopulations.
